davincifire.headline: A small account carried by its parent company. More than half of what appears on the grid belongs to sister brands.
points: Visual style

Real phone video and photos, mostly shot on the factory floor under warehouse light. No renders, no branded templates. The on-screen text changes look from post to post, so the grid has no consistent visual identity.
Topics and series

One clear series: the President's Club dealer event, five posts in nine days. Around it, factory pride and Made in America. Their own posts push customisation: modular units, see-through models, glass heights, and the holographic electric line.
Video style
Reels run 22 to 89 seconds, most between 25 and 62. Licensed music on their own Reels, word by word subtitles whenever a person is on camera. No trending audio.
How they write

Medium captions in a confident product voice, few emojis. Hashtags dropped to zero on their four newest posts. One question to the audience in three months. Calls to action point to the link in bio or a phone number.
Who appears
Company staff and leadership, including the president, a recurring presenter, and dealers. One trade partner. No designers, no influencers, no customer homes.
Community
They do not reply to comments. In five posts checked there was not one answer, including two where people asked about installers.
davincifire.read: This account talks to dealers and the trade, not to homeowners. The content that travels is the group's, not DaVinci's: the 90 second factory tour and the gas ban explainer were seen two to three times more than anything DaVinci posted alone. Posting has no rhythm, with a two week silence followed by five posts in one event.
borrow: A fast factory tour. It is their most watched post by a wide margin, and we have a factory story to tell too.
An explainer on a topic people are already worried about (their gas ban video). It drew the most comments of the period.
Word by word subtitles on every Reel with a person speaking.
gaps: They never answer comments. Replying, especially to where to buy and installer questions, is an easy way to look better than them.
No homeowner content at all: no real homes, no designers, no before and after.
No consistent look. A recognisable template would stand out next to them.

modernflamesusa.headline: The brand barely posts. Its grid is other people's work: creators, dealers and customers showing Modern Flames in real homes.
points: Visual style
Real homes in warm interior light, shot by home creators, dealers and DIY customers. The single post the brand made itself is a polished product image that looks like a render. No branded template.
Topics and series

No series. The repeating pattern is the dealer showcase: one stone dealer appears twice with the same caption formula, location, a line to book a consultation, and eight or nine hashtags. The rest is finished rooms and installs.
Video style
Every Reel belongs to a creator: their voice or original audio, their editing, their on-screen text. Lengths go from 16 seconds to over two minutes.
How they write
The brand's own caption is long and editorial, points to an article, and uses no hashtags. Partner captions are short with four to nine hashtags. No questions to the audience.
Who appears
A home and design creator, a DIY creator, two dealers, a woodworker who bought the product. The brand's own people never appear.
Community
They do reply, but only with emoji or two words of praise on the posts they are tagged in.
modernflamesusa.read: Modern Flames lets its customers and dealers do the talking. It costs them almost nothing and it works when a creator has reach: one creator Reel was seen 23,600 times on an account with 2,500 followers, nine times its own audience. The weakness is the same thing. With seven posts in three months and one of their own, there is no rhythm and no brand voice, so the account depends entirely on who decides to tag them.
borrow: Shared posts with home creators. Their two creator Reels are the most watched content of any account read so far, far above anything a brand posted alone.
Real homes over product shots. Finished rooms from customers and dealers are what gets watched.
Dealer showcases with a clear next step, such as booking a consultation.
gaps: Almost silent: seven posts in three months. A steady weekly rhythm already puts us ahead.
No voice of their own. Nothing explains the product, the technology or how to choose.
Replies are emoji only. Real answers to real questions would stand out.

valorfireplaces.headline: The most disciplined account so far and the least watched. A calendar that runs like clockwork, built on photos almost nobody reacts to.
points: Visual style

Single photos of bright, professionally shot rooms with the fireplace as the centre, indoors and outdoors. No text on the image, no branded frame. A few images look generated, and one dealer post carries Instagram's generated content label.
Topics and series

The clearest editorial structure of the accounts read. Seasonal posts (first day of fall, Labour Day, October), education openers that repeat (Did you know, Myth vs Fact), and technology explainers that return every few weeks: HeatShift, HeatSplit, AutoFire, No Power No Problem. Two product launches in the period.
Video style
Almost none. Three Reels in three months, each 31 to 41 seconds of slow product and flame footage with original audio and no text on screen.
How they write
Long, calm, educational captions of three to five paragraphs, few emojis. Nearly every one closes with link in the bio and four to seven hashtags. Questions to the audience are rare.
Who appears
Models in lifestyle photos and three dealers through shared posts. No designers, no creators, no installers, no real customers.
Community
They do not reply to comments. Five posts checked, no answer on any of them.
valorfireplaces.read: Valor runs Instagram as a scheduled brochure. About two posts a week, on the same weekdays, in the early afternoon, many of them timed to the exact hour, which points to a scheduling tool. Every post follows the same path: teach something, then send people to find a dealer or get a quote. It is consistent and well organised, and it earns almost nothing: zero to two comments per post, and their own Reels reach 560 to 630 views on 4,300 followers. The lesson is that rhythm alone does not create attention. The format does.
borrow: The calendar itself: fixed days, fixed time, seasonal hooks planned ahead. It is the one thing the other accounts lack.
Named education formats that repeat, such as Did you know and Myth vs Fact. Easy to recognise and easy to produce.
One clear next step on every post, find a dealer or get a quote.
gaps: Almost no video. Three Reels in three months, while Reels are what gets watched on every other account.
Photos with long captions get no reaction: zero to two comments per post.
No people. No creators, no designers, no customers, and no replies to comments.

napoleonfireplace.headline: The only account run as a real programme: a paid council of designers, a magazine partnership and a launch calendar, posted almost every day.
points: Visual style

Two looks side by side. Calm, warm-wood interiors for product posts, many of which look like renders. And a fixed Design Council template: marble background, the designer's round photo with a yellow name tag, a yellow headline in capitals and the Napoleon logo. It is the only branded template among the accounts read.
Topics and series

Design Council is the backbone: five paid designers giving one design tip each, once or twice a week, as Reels and as template posts, always under the same hashtag. Around it runs a launch cycle that repeats for every new product: a teaser, the launch, then a second post. Four launches followed that pattern in three months. A third strand is a partnership with a home magazine.
Video style

Designer Reels are 16 to 75 seconds with the designer talking to camera inside the Design Council frame. Product Reels are short, 17 to 27 seconds, flames and music only. Partner Reels are the longest, over a minute.
How they write

Long, structured captions with sub headers and tips. Always exactly three hashtags. Launch posts close with learn more through the link in our bio. Questions to the audience are rare and come mostly from partners.
Who appears

Paid interior designers, a well known TV builder, a home decor magazine, three dealers, a lighting brand and a builder. A PR agency is tagged on the paid posts, which suggests the programme is managed for them.
Community
They do not reply on their own posts. They do leave one reply on partner Reels.
napoleonfireplace.read: Napoleon buys its reach, and it works. A Reel with a paid designer is seen about nine times more than one of their own product Reels, and the magazine Reels go higher still: the top one reached 63,300 views on an account with 16,300 followers. Without those, Napoleon looks like everyone else: product Reels sit around 1,000 to 1,300 views and photos draw zero to three comments. So the lesson is not that Napoleon makes better content. It is that a face people trust, talking about design rather than about the product, is what gets watched. Their volume is also far above the rest, about four posts a week, weekends included.
borrow: A small council of named designers with a fixed format. It gives them a weekly series, a recognisable look and borrowed audiences at once.
Design advice first, product second. Their most watched Reels are about proportions, lighting and planning a room, with the fireplace as part of the answer.
The launch cycle: teaser, launch, follow up. Each new product gets three moments instead of one.
A media partner. Three magazine Reels together were seen about thirteen times more than all eight of their own product Reels.
gaps: Their own content is weak without the paid names. Product Reels and photos get the same low numbers as everyone else.
They do not answer comments on their own posts.
Many interiors look rendered. Real homes and real installs would feel more honest next to them.
The reach depends on budget. If the programme stops, the numbers go with it.

dimplex_northamerica.headline: We have the largest audience of the five and a feed built around the product. The Reels that travel are the ones our partners make.
points: Visual style

Two looks. A spec sheet template on a beige background, with the product in the centre and thin lines pointing at its features. And clean interior scenes, many of them render style. Our Reels are short flame close ups on black.
Topics and series

Product by product: Ignite Quest, Ignite Bold, Ignite Ultra, Vital, Revillusion, Storm Surround, the Optimyst range. One clear run around IDS Vancouver in September (teaser, giveaway, a Reel from the show, a partner tie in) and the summer promotion in July.
Video style

Six Reels in three months, four of them ours. Ours run 15 to 48 seconds and show flames and product only, with music or original audio. No voice and no text on screen. The two partner Reels have a person talking and text on screen.
How we write
A one line headline, one paragraph on features, four or five hashtags. Few emojis, no questions to the audience. A call to action appears only for availability or a promotion.
Who appears
Almost never a person. Partners in the period: a stone brand, a distributor, a trade show, an apartment project, a DIY creator and a dealer. That same dealer also publishes with Napoleon.
Community
No replies to comments in the five posts checked.
dimplex_northamerica.read: Our account works as a product catalogue. It is consistent and on brand, and it reaches very few of the 19,400 people who follow us: a typical Reel we make ourselves is seen about 775 times. The two Reels made by partners tell a different story. A dealer showing a 120 inch Opti-myst install reached 32,800 views, around forty times our typical Reel, and a DIY creator reached 3,455. The audience is there. What it responds to is a real person showing a real installation, not the product on its own.
borrow: Partner Reels. Our two best results of the period both came from someone else's account, a dealer and a creator.
The largest follower base of the five accounts, 19,400, ahead of Napoleon.
A real series around IDS Vancouver, with a teaser, a giveaway and a Reel from the floor.
A recognisable spec sheet template that nobody else uses.
gaps: Put a person on camera. None of our own Reels has a voice or a face, and those are the ones that get watched everywhere else.
Make more Reels. Six of our eighteen posts were Reels, and only four were ours.
Answer comments. No account of the five does it on its own posts, so it is an open lane.
Give every post a next step: where to buy, find a dealer, see it at a showroom.

_overall.headline: Across five accounts the product alone does not get watched. A person with their own audience does.
findings: Own product content has a ceiling
Reels a brand makes about its own product land between roughly 400 and 2,800 views on every account that makes them, whether it has 3,000 followers or 19,400.
Every breakout has a person behind it
Paid designers for Napoleon (41,600 views), a home magazine (63,300), a decor creator for Modern Flames (23,600), a dealer for us (32,800). The same dealer delivered 32,600 for Napoleon.
Posting more is not the lever
Valor posts on a strict schedule, about twice a week, and gets the lowest numbers. Modern Flames barely posts and has the most watched Reel per follower.
We have the audience, not the reach
Dimplex has the most followers of the five, and a typical Reel we make ourselves is seen about 775 times, around 4 views for every 100 followers.
No account answers comments on its own posts, and all five hide their like counts.
plan: Lead with partners. Line up shared Reels with dealers and home creators every month. One dealer Reel brought forty times the views of our typical one.
Put a face and a voice in our own Reels. Design advice first, product as part of the answer.
Create one named weekly series with a fixed look, the way Napoleon runs its Design Council.
Keep a calendar with fixed days, and give each launch three moments: teaser, launch, follow up.
Answer every comment. It costs nothing and no competitor does it.
